html:
By the time I finish this paragraph, there will be three minutes left before my zodiac year begins. (Every twelve years your birth sign comes round again; mine is the Dragon.)

My last zodiac year, 2012, feels as if it was only a short while ago. My wife and I wore matching red hoodies that my mom bought us. I was in the first year of my master’s, preparing to go abroad, and had scored 104 on the TOEFL. That year I got my driver’s license, and at the end of the year I went abroad for the first time. Grandma was still alive. We spent New Year at the little home she shared with my eldest uncle, Mom’s brother; we played mahjong, and I took lots of photos with Grandma. She wasn’t so confused back then, and she cared about how she looked. When I took her picture just after she woke up, she frowned and said, “My face is all puffy from sleeping, what are you taking pictures for?” and kept smoothing down her sleep-tousled hair.

We played mahjong all day at Second Aunt’s (she is Dad’s sister) and got home after eight. The three of us made dumplings and started eating soon after nine. Dad suggested we eat on the sofa so we could watch the Spring Festival Gala, the state TV variety show that plays in most Chinese homes on New Year’s Eve. Mom said she couldn’t remember how many years it had been since the three of us had New Year’s Eve dinner at home together. My guess is 2013, the year after my last zodiac year. After I moved abroad, the only New Year I came back for was 2019, and we spent it at my eldest aunt’s in the countryside, with my eldest cousin, my youngest male cousin and their families, and Grandma.

After lunch I went downstairs by myself to cool off; it was far too hot at Second Aunt’s. Dad doesn’t get it either: why not turn off a radiator or two, instead of running them all full blast and then opening the windows? My theory: the heating bill is a flat rate. I walked along the half-melted snow. There weren’t many people on the street; every now and then came a burst of firecrackers. I thought of New Years more than a decade ago, which were the stage for our pool-playing prowess. Every day we’d be in and out of the pool hall, never winning or losing much, our energy boundless, and we kept it up until we all had families and went our separate ways. I lit a cigarette and walked toward the mountain. Winter in my hometown and a cigarette are a perfect match; together they work like a time machine.

Mom just came in to tell me to go to bed. So that she can sleep soundly, I’m going to close the laptop, turn off the light and carry on the fight on my phone. Night! Happy Year of the Dragon!
